# SK4030 — The collection's own method answers this faster than the LINQ extension

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`List<T>` and `ImmutableList<T>` declare `Find`, `Exists` and `TrueForAll`; the `Enumerable` extension that answers the same question allocates an enumerator to do it.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Performance |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S6602, S6603, S6605, S6617 |

## Why

`FirstOrDefault`, `Any` and `All` are written against `IEnumerable<T>`, so they allocate an enumerator, drive it through `MoveNext` and call the predicate through it. `Find`, `Exists` and `TrueForAll` are members of the list, so they walk the backing array with an index and allocate nothing. The delegate is the same object under two names — `Predicate<T>` and `Func<T, bool>` have identical signatures — so the substitution costs the reader nothing either. `Any(x => x == v)` is a third case of the same argument and the sharpest: `Contains(v)` needs no delegate at all, and the comparison ends up somewhere the reader can see it.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
var ready = items.FirstOrDefault(item => item.IsReady);
var anyReady = items.Any(item => item.IsReady);
var known = names.Any(name => name == wanted);
```

Write:

```csharp
var ready = items.Find(item => item.IsReady);
var anyReady = items.Exists(item => item.IsReady);
var known = names.Contains(wanted);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Every pair was checked on the empty sequence, which is where a substitution like this goes wrong, and none of them changes a return.** `All` is vacuously `true` and `TrueForAll` returns `true` over zero elements; `Any` and `Exists` are both `false`; `FirstOrDefault` and `Find` both return `default(T)` — for a value type as well, so neither throws where the other does not. `First`, `Single` and `SingleOrDefault` are deliberately outside the table, because `Find` returns a default where those throw. ⚠ **The receiver must be `List<T>` or `ImmutableList<T>` as the semantic model resolves it**, never a type that merely has a member of the right name. A set carries an `IEqualityComparer<T>`, so `HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase).Contains(v)` and `Any(x => x == v)` genuinely disagree, and that is the false positive this restriction exists to prevent. ⚠ The `Any(x => x == v)` rewrite additionally requires an element type whose default equality comparer *is* its `==`: `string`, the integral types, `char`, `bool`, `decimal` and any `enum`. `double` and `float` are excluded because `NaN == NaN` is false where `EqualityComparer<double>.Default.Equals(NaN, NaN)` is true and `-0.0 == 0.0` is true where `Equals` is false; reference types are excluded because `==` may be identity, or an operator somebody wrote. The compared value must also be a name path or a literal, so that moving it out of the lambda does not change how many times it is evaluated. ⚠ The predicate must be written as a lambda or an anonymous method. A `Func<T, bool>` variable does not convert to `Predicate<T>` — the fix would be CS1503 — and a method group is left alone as the cheaper miss. ⚠ **One real behavioural difference is recorded rather than guarded**: `Enumerable.Any` iterates through the list's enumerator, which checks the version field, so a predicate that mutates the list mid-scan throws `InvalidOperationException`; `Exists` walks the array and does not. A predicate that mutates the collection it is scanning is a defect either way, and building a guard for it would mean proving a lambda pure.
